4. The plaintiffs' case in short is that the suit premises originally belonged to one Binodi Lal Biswas a practising Mukhtiar at Dinajpur and the plaintiffs acquired the same from the said Binodi Lal Biswaw in exchange of their Indian property Binodi Lal Biswas executed a power of attorney in favour of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit premises and some other properties. The aforesaid document was registered as deed No. 8058 on 12-5-1961 at the Sub-Registry Office of Dinajpur. The plaintiffs first let out the suit premises to Bibhuti Bhusan Deb father of the defendant and after Bibhutis death in 1971 let out the premises to the defendant at a monthly rent of Taka 30.00 from March, 1972 and  subsequently the rent was enhanced to Taka 60.00 per month. The defendant was a monthly tenant under the plaintiffs in respect of the suit premises. He regularly paid rent to the plaintiffs upto March, 1979 and thereafter, he defaulted. The defendant was a habitual defaulter. The plaintiffs were in bonafide requirement of the suit premises for their own use as plaintiff No. 1 Rabiul Alam subsequently became an Advocate. The plaintiffs issued notice under section 106 and 111 of the Transfer of Property Act by registered post to the defendant through their lawyer determining the relationship of landlord and tenant and demanding vacant possession of the suit premises on the expiry of the Month of September, 1982. The defendant received the notice in time but did not vacate the premises hence the suit. 

 5. The defendant opposite party contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations and assertions made in the plaint stating inter alia that the plaintiffs had no cause of action: that the suit was not maintainable; that the SCC Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit; that there was no relationship of landlord and tenant between them; that the suit was bad for defect of parties;: that the plaintiffs had no right, title and interest in the suit premises; that Benodi Lal Biswas the original owner of the suit property abandoned the same as some ghostly occurrence took place in the said house and lived in a nearby house; that having found the house vacant the defendant's father Bibhuti Bhusan entered into the said house in 1947 just after the partition and lived therein with his family till his death in 1971; that the defendant was neither a tenant nor a licencee under anybody; that after the death of his father the defendant and the members of his family continued to live in the suit premises, that Binodi Lal left Dinajpur for India that in collusion with some influential persons the plaintiffs forged a power of attorney purported to have been executed by Binodi Lal Biswas in order to grab the valuable property, that after the promulgation of Martial Law in 1975 Kotwali Police having been influenced by the plaintiffs threatened the defendant with dispossession and eviction if they failed to recognise the plaintiffs as their landlord; that in order to avoid forcible eviction the defendant put his signature on a rent receipt and recognised the plaintiffs as his landlords and once he deposited Taka 40.00 only with the House Rent Controller in favour of the plaintiffs but subsequently withdrew the said case; that the ADC (Rev) Dinajpur illegally executed a deed of exchange for registration in favour of the plaintiffs; that the  plaintiffs have no right title interest and possession in the suit premises and hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 6. The learned SCC Judge framed as many as 6 issues namely 1) was the suit maintainable in its present form 2) was the defendant a tenant under the plaintiffs 3) was the defendant a habitual defaulter 4) were the plaintiffs in bonafide requirement of the suit premises 5) had the plaintiffs incidental title in the suit premises and 6) what other relief or reliefs were the plaintiffs entitled to? The plaintiffs examined 4 PWs in support of their case while the defendant examined 8 DWs and having considered the evidence on record the learned SCC Judge by judgment and order dated 30-6-87 returned the plaint for filing in the proper court holding inter alia that he defendant did not attorne the plaintiffs as his landlords, that there was no relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties that the suit was bad for defect of parties, and that the suit was not maintainable as a complicated question of title was involved in the suit and thus decided almost all the vital issues against the plaintiffs 

 7. Mr MA Wahab Miah learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners submits that since the defendant opposite party recognised the plaintiffs as landlords by payment of rent (Ext. 5 series) and by depositing rent before the Rent Controller in Miscellanea Case No. 97 of 1979 (Ext. 10 (a) and since PW3 Rafiquddin Ahmed deposed to the effect. 

 9. Mr Wahab further submits that having got the deed of exchange validated the plaintiffs mutated their names and paid rent (Ext. 3) and in that view of the matter the defendant who is a tenant under the plaintiffs is estopped from challenging the title of the plaintiffs and in support of this contention Mr Wahab cited the case of Haji Kasimuddin Mondal being dead his heirs Afroza Bewa and others vs. Md Jalaluddin Pramanik reported in 48 DLR (AD) 205. In the reported case it was held: 

 "In the instant case the suit is in essence and substantially a suit by the landlord for ejectment of his tenant. In such a case the question of title to the disputed premises is not relevant at all. Once a relationship of landlord and tenant is pleaded by the plaintiff the landlord cannot be thrown out of the Court of Small Causes on the plea of tenant's title on which the landlord's claim does not depend." 

 10. In the instant case the tenant does not claim title for himself rather he sets up a case that Binodi Lal never executed any deed of exchange in favour of the plaintiffs. In the reported case their Lordships further held that in the face of overwhelming evidence that there was relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiffs and the defendant the defendant could not raise any plea of the title to the disputed premises. It has been consistently held by the superior courts including this court that a tenant cannot set up title to a property of which he is a monthly tenant without surrendering possession to his landlord in view of section 116 of the Evidence Act. If the landlord can prove, as in the instant case, that the defendant was inducted by him on the disputed premises or that the defendant has attorned to him and has continued in possession on payment of rent after recognising him as the landlord he cannot turn round and deny the title of the said landlord. Reference may be made in this connection to the case of Abdus Sauar vs. Mohiuddin 38 DLR (AD) 97. His Lordship Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed J as his Lordship then was expounded the principle of law embodied in section 116 of the Evidence Act which runs thus; 

 Section 116 " The estoppel as described in this section is known as tenant's estoppel or estoppel by contract. This estoppel is founded upon a contract between the tenant and the landlord. It provides that when a person enters into possession of immovable property as a tenant of another person then neither he nor anybody claiming through him shall be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to deny the landlord's title however defective that title might be. This necessarily implies that in case the tenant sets up a claim of title in himself he shall firstly surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken it." 

 11. Mr Muhammad Jamiruddin Sircar, learned Counsel appearing for the opposite party submits that in view of the finding of the trial Court that the case involved a question of title the same should not be tried by the SCC, Court rather by a competent civil court. But on a reference to the evidence and the documents mentioned above I am unable to accept this contention of the learned Counsel for the opposite party inasmuch as the suit being between an alleged landlord and an alleged tenant for enforcement of certain rights of the landlord the simple question which is to be tried in such a suit is whether there is existence of any relationship of a landlord and a tenant as has been established by PWs 3.4 and 5 inasmuch as by the rent receipt Ext. 5 series and the House Rent Countrol case filed by the defendant being Misc. Case No. 97 of 1997 (Rent Control) it was proved that the defendant was a tenant under the plaintiffs. In such a case the question of title to the premises in question is not relevant at all. The position of law is based upon the rule of evidence regarding the doctrine of estoppel as embodied in section 116 of the Evidence Act which has been elaborately discussed in 48 DLR(AD) 205. 

 12. The second point argued by Mr Sircar is that the deed of exchange should have been between a Hindu migrant and a Muslim refugee/expelee of India but that is absent in the instant case. In view of the enquiry conducted by the Deputy Commissioner, Dinajpur and the resultant report as to the genuineness of the deed of exchange and the validation of the same by the Deputy Commissioner Dinajpur and the validation of the same having been accepted by the Deputy Commissioner, Dinajpur in the face of objection raised by the defendant (which was turned down) the legality of the exchange cannot be challenged, Furthermore, against the order of executed and registered in India why should there by validation, the defendant moved the concerned any bar in getting it executed in Bangladesh or in the Ministry but that was also rejected.  In that view of then East Pakistan  the matter the second contention raised by Mr Sircar can not also be accepted. Mr Sircar further submits that the father of the defendant namely Bibhuti Bhushan entered the suit premises in the year 1947 and died on 20-2-71. Moreover defendant Bidhan Kumar Deb was born in the suit premises in the year 1948. So the question of his induction as a tenant does not arise. This contention of Mr Sircar is contradicted by the statement made in the house rent control case being Misc Case No. 97 of 1979 (Rent Control) wherein it has been stated that Bibhuti Bhushan entered into the suit premises in 1972. 

 13. The next contention of Mr Sircar is that the signature of Bidhan Kumar Deb on the counter foil of the rent receipt is disputed but on a reference to the chircuit (চিরকুট) Ext.4 acknowledging payment of rent for the month of October and November. 1977, the signature of Bidhan Kumar dated 28-11-77 thereon witnessed by Abdul Halim Sarder who is none else than the Sub-Editor of the Daily lanamat of which Bidhan Kumar is the editor, (and this signature of Bidhan) tallied with Ext. No. 5(21), 5 (29) and 5(39). So there is no scope for saying that the signature appearing on Ext. 4 and 5 series are not of Bidhan Kumar. Mr Sircar lastly submits that the signature of Bidhan Kumar was obtained by intimidation, threat and coereion in abnormal situation then prevailing in the country. But on a reference to the Proclamation dated 7th of April.  1979 it appears that Lieutenant General Ziaur Rahman was elected President of Bangladesh under the Constitution held on 3rd June. 1978 and entered upon the office of President and whereas further continuance of Martial Law was no longer necessary in the national interest it was withdrawn. Mr Sircar also submits that both the plaintiffs and the defendants being residents of Dinajpur town, Binodi Lal is alleged to have given power of attorney from Dinajpur town and the Power of Attorney was registered in Dinajpur as such it is not a case of exchange with the Indian property. This submission, I am constrained to say is a fallacious one inasmuch  as if power of attorney and deed of exchange can be executed and registered in India why should there by any bar in getting it executed in Bangladesh or in the then East Pakistan. 

 15. From a reading of section 23 of the Small Cause Courts Act it is clear that the word May in section 23 is not mandatory. When in a suit heard by a Small Cause Court any complicated question as to title to immovable property is involved it would be wiser course to act under section 23 as decided in the case of Lala Singh vs. Mohipal Singh 1889 AWN 149. But in the instant case I do not find any question of title involved let alone a complicated question of title because the tenant himself does not set up a title for himself, he merely alleges that the original owner Benodi Lal did not exchange the property with the plaintiffs. The trial Court held that mere payment of rent is no recognition by the tenant of his landlord but as has already been referred to the signature appearing in Ext. 4 ie chircuit   is exactly the same as in Ext. 5 (21), 5(29) and 5(39). 

 16. As regards the filing of the Misc. Case  No. 97 of 1979 (Rent Control) recognizing the plaintiffs as the landlord, the learned trial Court wrongly held that it was filed on the advice given by Mr Amanuallh Senior (Advocate) to the defendant Bidhan Kumar only to avoid eviction because at that time the country was going through abnormal situation and that the said Mr Amanullah and other Advocates named by the defendants were not examined by the plaintiffs to disprove the assertion made by the defendant that he had to file the rent control case only to avoid eviction. This finding of section 101 and 102 of Evidence Act. The assertion of the defendant has to be proved by him and not by the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs have no duty to prove an assertion made by the defendant. 

 17. Paragraph 14 of the written statement. Ext 4 the chircuit (চিরকুট) the rent receipt Ext. 5(21), 5 ,22) and 5(29), Misc. Case No. 97 of 1979 (Rent Control) Ext. 10(a) read together have made in a clear case of admission by the defendant that the plaintiffs are his landlord and, as such, he is estopped  from denying the plaintiffs title to the premises and in support of this contention Mr MA Wahab Miah learned Counsel for the petitioners cited the case of Hajee Abdus Sattar VS. Mahiuddin and ors reported in 1986 BLD(AD) 224.
